title: How To Be Consistent With Classroom Management gement/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that most teachers understand the importance of consistency but fail to actually practice it, instead enforcing consequences based on mood, situation, or the student involved. He presents consistency not as a matter of willpower but of confidence in a well-written classroom management plan followed every single time. The bulk of the article lists concrete consequences of inconsistency: it feels unfair to students, breeds resentment, erodes teacher respect, invites testing from challenging students, worsens overall behavior, harms learning, and leaves the teacher perpetually frustrated. He closes by rejecting the popular idea that different students warrant different standards, insisting that a single, objective plan applied to everyone (aside from documented IEP accommodations) is fairest and most effective.
points: Most teachers only 'kinda-sorta' follow their classroom management plan, adjusting consequences based on mood or circumstance rather than enforcing them uniformly.
Inconsistent enforcement is perceived by students as unfair and breeds resentment, especially toward students seen as getting special treatment.
Failing to follow through erodes teacher respect and invites more frequent testing and boundary-pushing from challenging students.
Weak accountability correlates directly with worse behavior, less learning, and greater teacher frustration and burnout.
A single, objective classroom management plan applied to every student (barring documented IEP accommodations) is fairer and more effective than individualized standards.
quotes: The solution is confidence, confidence in knowing that it is indeed best to follow through with your classroom management plan every single time.
To enforce your agreed-upon consequences sometimes and not others is grossly unfair to your students.
Whenever you say you’re going to do something and don’t do it, you lose a layer of respect from your students.
When your most challenging students learn that you’re not so committed to enforcing consequences, that your classroom management plan is written in pencil, they’ll smell blood in the water.
Wherever there is weak accountability or semi accountability, behavior, respect, and kindness take a nosedive.

A well-written classroom management plan, on the other hand, followed as taught, modeled, and practiced, is fair to all students and never creates resentment, friction, and hard feelings between the teacher and her students.
